title: A rolling deployment triggers a rebalance for every pod restart — why does it hurt more than expected and how do you fix it?
shortTitle: A rolling deployment triggers a rebalance for every pod restart — why does it hurt more than expected, and how do you fix it?
topicTitle: A rolling deployment triggers a rebalance for every pod restart

s1_definition.profdef: A consumer group rebalance is the process where Kafka reassigns partitions among the live consumers in a group whenever membership changes. In a rolling deployment, each pod that stops and starts triggers a membership change, and with the default eager rebalance protocol every change makes all consumers stop consuming and give up all partitions before they are redistributed. During a rolling restart of N pods you therefore pay for 2N stop-the-world rebalances, each one pausing the whole group, which is why the impact is far larger than "one pod was briefly down."
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has ten tellers at ten counters, and customers are split across the counters by account number. Now the manager wants to send each teller, one at a time, for a five-minute coffee break. With the bad old rule, every single time one teller leaves OR comes back, ALL ten tellers must close their counters, drop their customer queues, huddle in the back room, and re-divide the entire customer list from scratch. Ten tellers leaving and returning means twenty of these full shutdowns. The bank grinds to a halt far longer than the coffee breaks themselves. The fix is a smarter rule where only the affected counter is touched and the other nine keep serving.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every pod stop and start is a separate membership change, and with eager rebalancing each one pauses the entire group, so a rolling deploy of N pods costs 2N stop-the-world pauses unless you switch to cooperative, sticky, and static-membership strategies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A consumer group rebalance is the process where Kafka reassigns partitions among the live consumers in a group whenever membership changes. In a rolling deployment, each pod that stops and starts triggers a membership change, and with the default eager rebalance protocol every change makes all consumers stop consuming and give up all partitions before they are redistributed. During a rolling restart of N pods you therefore pay for 2N stop-the-world rebalances, each one pausing the whole group, which is why the impact is far larger than "one pod was briefly down."

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has ten tellers at ten counters, and customers are split across the counters by account number. Now the manager wants to send each teller, one at a time, for a five-minute coffee break. With the bad old rule, every single time one teller leaves OR comes back, ALL ten tellers must close their counters, drop their customer queues, huddle in the back room, and re-divide the entire customer list from scratch. Ten tellers leaving and returning means twenty of these full shutdowns. The bank grinds to a halt far longer than the coffee breaks themselves. The fix is a smarter rule where only the affected counter is touched and the other nine keep serving.

**One line to remember:** Every pod stop and start is a separate membership change, and with eager rebalancing each one pauses the entire group, so a rolling deploy of N pods costs 2N stop-the-world pauses unless you switch to cooperative, sticky, and static-membership strategies.

sections.s2_technical:
The core reason a rolling deployment hurts is the default rebalance protocol. Historically Kafka used the eager assignment protocol, where on any membership change every consumer revokes all of its partitions, the group coordinator recomputes the assignment, and every consumer re-joins. This is often called a stop-the-world rebalance because no partition in the group is being consumed during the revoke-and-reassign window. During a rolling deployment, Kubernetes terminates pod 1 (one rebalance), the new pod 1 joins (another rebalance), then pod 2 leaves and rejoins, and so on. The total is roughly two rebalances per pod.

The first fix is the cooperative sticky assignor. You set `partition.assignment.strategy` to `org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor`. With cooperative rebalancing, consumers only revoke the specific partitions that actually need to move, and they keep consuming everything else throughout. For example, if partition 7 must move from the departing pod to a surviving pod, only partition 7 pauses briefly; the other partitions never stop. A code snippet in a banking consumer looks like this: `props.put(ConsumerConfig.PARTITION_ASSIGNMENT_STRATEGY_CONFIG, "org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor");` and this single line removes most of the pain.

The second fix is static group membership, introduced through `group.instance.id`. Normally, when a consumer disconnects, the coordinator waits only `session.timeout.ms` and then declares it dead and rebalances. With a static member, you give each pod a stable identity such as `settlement-consumer-3`, and when that pod restarts within `session.timeout.ms`, the coordinator recognizes it as the same member returning and skips the rebalance entirely. For example, `props.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_INSTANCE_ID_CONFIG, "settlement-consumer-" + podOrdinal);` combined with a slightly larger `session.timeout.ms` means a quick pod restart causes zero rebalances. In Kubernetes you usually derive the ordinal from a StatefulSet pod name.

A senior-level nuance is that these two fixes stack. Static membership removes rebalances for restarts that finish quickly, and the cooperative assignor minimizes the cost of the rebalances that remain (scale-up, scale-down, or a pod that stays down too long). You also want to tune `session.timeout.ms` to comfortably exceed your pod's restart time, raise `max.poll.interval.ms` above your worst-case processing time so long batches are not mistaken for a dead consumer, and make sure your pod's `preStop` hook calls `consumer.close()` so the consumer leaves the group gracefully rather than timing out. Another nuance is partition-to-pod affinity: with the sticky assignor, a returning pod tends to get its old partitions back, so warmed-up local state and caches are preserved.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India we run a settlement consumer service as six pods, all in one consumer group called `settlement-group`, reading the `account.transfers` topic which has twelve partitions. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) generate transfer events that these pods process.

Problem 1 — every afternoon the platform team ships a new build with a rolling deployment. We noticed that during each deploy, end-to-end settlement latency spiked and consumer lag climbed sharply for about a minute, even though each individual pod was only down for a few seconds. This is exactly the eager-rebalance problem: each pod leaving and rejoining triggered a full stop-the-world rebalance, so six pods caused roughly twelve group-wide pauses, and during each pause nobody was settling Rajesh's or Priya's transfers.

Problem 2 — even after a pod came back, it was assigned different partitions than before, so its in-memory fraud-scoring cache was cold and the first few hundred transfers were slow. This is the stickiness problem: without a sticky assignor, partitions shuffle unnecessarily and local state is thrown away.

To demonstrate the behavior and the fix, our runnable demo will simulate a group coordinator and a set of consumer members. It will model two strategies side by side: the eager strategy, which revokes everything on any change, and the cooperative-plus-static strategy, which keeps surviving members running and skips rebalances for quick restarts. The demo classes are `RebalanceDemo` (the main driver), `GroupCoordinator` (tracks members and computes assignments and counts rebalances), `ConsumerMember` (a pod with a stable instance id), and `RebalanceStrategy` plus two implementations. We will roll-restart six members under each strategy and print the number of stop-the-world rebalances and how many partitions moved.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement-group
      enable-auto-commit: false
      properties:
        # Cooperative rebalancing: only move the partitions that must move
        partition.assignment.strategy: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
        # Stable identity per pod so a quick restart does NOT rebalance
        group.instance.id: ${POD_NAME}
        # Give a restarting pod time to come back before it is declared dead
        session.timeout.ms: 45000
        heartbeat.interval.ms: 10000
        # Allow slow batches without being kicked out
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: six pods named `settlement-consumer-0` through `settlement-consumer-5`, a topic with twelve partitions, and a rolling deployment that restarts each pod once.

Step 1: All six pods join `settlement-group`. The coordinator performs the initial assignment, giving each pod two partitions. At this point Rajesh's and Priya's transfers are being consumed normally across all twelve partitions.

Step 2 (eager path): The deploy terminates `settlement-consumer-0`. Under eager, the coordinator tells all remaining pods to revoke every partition. Consumption stops group-wide. The new `settlement-consumer-0` joins, and again all pods revoke and reassign. That is two stop-the-world rebalances for one pod, and nothing is consumed during either pause.

Step 3 (eager path continued): This repeats for pods 1 through 5. The total is twelve stop-the-world rebalances, and the partitionsMoved counter climbs because every rebalance reshuffles all twelve partitions, discarding warm caches each time.

Step 4 (cooperative plus static path): The deploy terminates `settlement-consumer-0`, but because it has a static `group.instance.id` and restarts within `session.timeout.ms`, the coordinator recognizes the returning member and performs no rebalance at all. The surviving five pods never stop consuming.

Step 5 (cooperative plus static path continued): Each of the six pods restarts the same way, so the stop-the-world count stays at zero and partitionsMoved stays at zero. Rajesh's and Priya's transfers keep settling throughout the deploy.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-24 21:40:01] [INFO] === Strategy 1: EAGER (stop-the-world on every change) ===
[2026-10-24 21:40:01] [INFO] EAGER total stop-the-world rebalances = 12, partitions moved = 156
[2026-10-24 21:40:01] [INFO] === Strategy 2: COOPERATIVE + STATIC MEMBERSHIP ===
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rolling Deploy: restart settlement-consumer-0 .. 5 (group of 6, topic 12 partitions)
    │
    ├─ EAGER PROTOCOL                               ├─ COOPERATIVE + STATIC MEMBERSHIP
    │  pod-0 terminates                             │  pod-0 terminates
    │    │ coordinator: revoke ALL from ALL          │    │ static id known, within session.timeout
    │    ▼ STOP-THE-WORLD #1 (group idle)            │    ▼ NO rebalance (5 pods keep running)
    │  pod-0 rejoins                                 │  pod-0 rejoins fast (same group.instance.id)
    │    │ coordinator: revoke ALL from ALL          │    │ coordinator: welcome back same member
    │    ▼ STOP-THE-WORLD #2 (group idle)            │    ▼ NO rebalance, pod-0 regains old partitions
    │  ... repeat for pods 1..5                      │  ... repeat for pods 1..5
    ▼                                                ▼
  12 stop-the-world pauses                          0 stop-the-world pauses
  all 12 partitions reshuffled each time            0 partitions moved, caches stay warm
  lag spikes, settlement latency jumps              lag flat, Rajesh/Priya transfers never pause
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A consumer group rebalance is how Kafka redistributes partitions among live consumers whenever group membership changes. The reason a rolling deployment hurts far more than people expect is the default eager rebalance protocol, which is a stop-the-world operation. On any membership change, every consumer revokes all of its partitions, the coordinator recomputes the assignment, and everyone rejoins. During a rolling deploy each pod stops and then starts, so a group of N pods pays for roughly two of these stop-the-world rebalances per pod, and during every one of them no partition in the group is being consumed, which is why lag and latency spike for far longer than the actual pod downtime.

In my work on the National Bank of India settlement service we saw exactly this. We ran six consumer pods on a twelve-partition transfers topic, and every afternoon deploy caused a visible lag spike even though each pod was only down for a few seconds. The root cause was twelve stop-the-world rebalances per deploy, plus cold caches because partitions were reshuffled every single time.

The fix has two parts that stack together. First, I switched the partition assignment strategy to the cooperative sticky assignor, so that during an unavoidable rebalance only the partitions that actually need to move are paused while every other partition keeps being consumed. Second, I gave each pod a stable group instance id to enable static membership, and I raised the session timeout comfortably above the pod restart time. With static membership, a pod that restarts quickly is recognized as the same member returning, so the coordinator skips the rebalance entirely. I also made sure the pod's preStop hook closes the consumer so it leaves the group gracefully, and I tuned the max poll interval above our worst-case processing time so slow batches are not mistaken for dead consumers.

The result was that a full rolling deploy went from roughly a dozen group-wide pauses down to zero rebalances for quick restarts, settlement latency stayed flat throughout the deploy, and because the sticky assignor returns a pod to its old partitions, our fraud-scoring caches stayed warm. The lesson I give juniors is simple: measure the rebalance count during a deploy, and if it is high, reach for cooperative sticky assignment and static membership before you blame the application code.
